messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Paramedic
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 35

**Vignette: Mr. R., Age 61, South Asian Male, Paramedic**

Mr. R. sits at the edge of the chair, hands resting on his knees, his breathing shallow. He speaks with a measured calm that seems to cost him something. He has been a paramedic for thirty-four years. Three years ago, during a call to a small chemical processing plant, he was the first responder to enter a maintenance shed where a valve had ruptured. He did not have full hazmat gear—only a surgical mask and gloves—because the dispatch had reported a “minor gas leak.” Inside the shed, the air felt thick and sweet, and within seconds his eyes burned and his throat clamped shut. He carried the unconscious plant worker outside, coughing and gasping. The worker survived; Mr. R. spent two days in the hospital with chemical pneumonitis.

Now, he no longer works on the ambulance. He took an early retirement last year because he could not tolerate the smell of diesel, the hiss of an oxygen tank, or the sight of protective suits hanging in the station. “Something inside me just… shifted,” he says, looking at the floor.

The exposure itself was acute, but the lingering effects are written into his daily life. He avoids any location that might have a chemical odor—cleaning aisles at the grocery store, the laundry room at home if his wife uses bleach. His wife, Meera, has stopped using any scented products; she knows that even the smell of her cooking oil can make him stop mid-sentence, his eyes darting toward the kitchen. He does not talk about the event, but he replays it silently: the sweet smell, the burning, the feeling of his lungs closing. Often at night, around 2:00 AM, he wakes with a sensation of suffocation, his hands grabbing at his throat. He then spends an hour walking the house, checking the stove, opening windows, circling the driveway to be sure there is no leak.

At family gatherings, Mr. R. sits apart. He used to be the storyteller, the one who cracked jokes about calls gone wrong. Now his younger brother’s laugh feels grating, and he leaves the room when the conversation turns to health, hospitals, or any mention of sickness. Meera has told the therapist that he “disappears” for hours in the garden, not tending plants, just standing still. She also notes that he has become rigid about his own health—checking his oxygen saturation three times a day, hoarding inhalers, and refusing to let her use any aerosol spray within fifty feet of him.

His sleep is fractured by nightmares, but not the obvious kind. He dreams of colorless mists, of trying to breathe through wet cloth, of people dissolving into yellow fog. He does not share these; he simply says, “I don’t sleep well.” His appetite is reduced—he avoids spicy foods, claiming they “burn,” though his stomach is fine. He has lost twelve pounds over eighteen months.

At his last paramedic reunion, a colleague mentioned a “chemical spill drill” coming up. Mr. R. felt a jolt of heat along his arms, his mouth went dry, and he excused himself to the restroom. He stood in the stall for ten minutes, staring at his hands, telling himself he was fine. He left without saying goodbye and has not spoken to that colleague since.

The PCL-5 score of 35 reflects his moderate but persistent distress. He does not wish to call this “PTSD.” To him, it is “just a bad memory.” He still drives his own car but takes back roads, avoiding the freeway near the chemical plant. He checks his phone repeatedly for alerts from the fire department, even though he is no longer on call. His world has narrowed to a small radius of safety: his home, his garden, his wife’s careful routine.

In session, he keeps his arms crossed. He waits for the therapist to tell him what is wrong, but he also fears hearing it. “I thought I was tougher than this,” he says. “I was the one who helped people. Now I can’t even walk past a paint store.”
